A Dacorogna-Moser construction of transport maps on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with application to geodesics on the space of couplings

Louis-Pierre Chaintron    Matteo Picco Affiliation: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Institute of Mathematics, 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland.
Abstract

Abstract

A seminal work by Dacorogna and Moser introduced a way of constructing regular transport maps from a probability distribution on a bounded domain to another one. In this work, we extend this construction to the whole ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for strictly asymptotically log-concave measures, a wide class of distributions that encompasses Lipschitz-perturbations of log-concave measures. A key feature of our extension is to produce transport maps that satisfy global regularity bounds. We then leverage this construction to study geodesics in the space of probability measures on a product set with imposed marginal laws (couplings), for which we derive optimality conditions, answering an open question in a recent work by Conforti, Lacker and Pal. Taking inspiration from Brenier’s variational model for incompressible fluids and its regularization, we further introduce an entropic regularization of the geodesic problem, which can be seen as the Schrödinger bridge problem on the space of couplings, for which we also derive optimality conditions. We eventually study convergence of minimizers as the regularization vanishes, and we prove convergence of the related Lagrange multipliers. Our approach involves proving uniform-in-time global regularity estimates on elliptic and parabolic equations on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, by exploiting the structure of asymptotically log-concave measures using the probabilistic notion of reflection coupling.

1 Introduction

The construction of regular transport maps has attracted significant attention in recent years, motivated by both theoretical and applied considerations. On the theoretical side, such maps play a central role in extending functional inequalities, including Poincaré and log-Sobolev inequalities, to broader classes of probability measures [42, 51, 34]. From a computational perspective, regular transport maps provide an effective framework for sampling from complex probability distributions [49, 25]. Indeed, a Lipschitz transport map from a simple reference measure – such as a Gaussian – to a target measure enables sampling from the latter while providing explicit error estimates in terms of the Lipschitz constant of the map. This principle is fundamental in modern generative machine learning, where the objective is to efficiently generate samples from prescribed probability distributions. Many approaches have been developed to enlarge the class of target measures that can be handled and to improve the efficiency of sampling, including diffusion models [39, 61], flow matching [46] and stochastic interpolants [2]. We refer the reader to Subsection 1.2 for a more detailed overview of these methods and their connections to regular transport maps.

The seminal work [28] by Dacorogna and Moser constructed Hölder-continuous transport maps between probability densities ff and gg on a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, under mild regularity assumptions on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, ff and gg. In the particular case where ff is the uniform probability density on Ω\Omega and the target is g=(1+φ)⋅fg=(1+\varphi)\cdot f with ∫Ωφ⁡(x)​f​(x)​𝑑x=0\int_{\Omega}\varphi(x)f(x)\mathrm{d}x=0, the transport map in [28, Lemma 3] is built from a flow (ρs)s∈[0,1](\rho_{s})_{s\in[0,1]} of probability measures that is a weak solution of the transport equation

∂sρs+∇⋅(ρs​vs)=0,ρ0=f​d​x,ρ1=g​d​x,\partial_{s}\rho_{s}+\nabla\cdot(\rho_{s}v_{s})=0,\quad\rho_{0}=f\mathrm{d}x,\quad\rho_{1}=g\mathrm{d}x, (1)

for a suitably chosen regular vector field (vs)s∈[0,1](v_{s})_{s\in[0,1]}. The transport map T:ℝd→ℝdT:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying

ρ1=T#​ρ0\rho_{1}=T_{\#}\rho_{0}

is then given by the flow generated by (vs)s∈[0,1](v_{s})_{s\in[0,1]} at time s=1s=1. A key simplifying assumption for choosing (vs)s∈[0,1](v_{s})_{s\in[0,1]} is

ρs=(1+s​φ)⋅f,vs=−∇u1+s​φ,\rho_{s}=(1+s\varphi)\cdot f,\qquad v_{s}=-\frac{\nabla u}{1+s\varphi},

which reduces (1) to solving the system

{Δ​u=φ, in ​Ω,∂u∂ν=0, on ​∂Ω,\begin{cases}\Delta u=\varphi,&\text{ in }\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=0,&\text{ on }\partial\Omega,\end{cases} (2)

the choice of the Neumann boundary condition ensuring that the resulting transport map leaves the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega invariant [28, Theorem 1]. The desired regularity for the transport map then results from proving estimates on the partial differential equation (PDE) (2). However, the estimates from [28, Theorem 1] explicitly depend on the boundedness of Ω\Omega, which prevents a direct extension of the construction to the whole ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

In this article, we propose an extension of the Dacorogna-Moser construction of transport maps, which is stated in Theorem 1.2 below, starting from a probability measure μ\mu on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Adapting the strategy from [28], we reduce the problem of constructing a transport map from μ\mu to (1+φ)⋅μ(1+\varphi)\cdot\mu to solving

Δψ+∇logμ⋅∇ψ=φ,∫ℝdψdμ=0,in ℝd,\Delta\psi+\nabla\log\mu\cdot\nabla\psi=\varphi,\qquad\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi\mathrm{d}\mu=0,\qquad\text{in }\mathbb{R}^{d}, (3)

in place of (2). The regularity of the transport map then follows from proving uniform regularity estimates on the solution of (3). To do so, we need to assume some decay for the tails of the measure μ\mu.

Throughout this work, our key assumption is the strict asymptotic log-concavity of the reference measure μ\mu. This assumption allows for non-log-concave measures, including Lipschitz perturbations of sufficiently coercive log-concave measures. To introduce it, we define the weak semiconvexity profile of a function f∈C1​(ℝd,ℝ)f\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}) as

κf​(r):=1r2​inf|x−y|=r⟨∇f​(x)−∇f​(y),x−y⟩,r>0.\kappa_{f}(r):=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\inf_{|x-y|=r}\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle,\quad r>0. (4)

It is classical that κf≥α\kappa_{f}\geq\alpha, for α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, is equivalent to ff being α\alpha-convex, i.e. x↦f⁡(x)−α2​|x|2x\mapsto f(x)-\frac{\alpha}{2}|x|^{2} being convex. The following definition is [20, Definition 1.1].

Definition 1.1 (Asymptotic convexity).

We say that a function f∈C1​(ℝd,ℝ)f\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}) is asymptotically convex if

lim infr→+∞κf​(r)≥0.\liminf_{r\to+\infty}\kappa_{f}(r)\geq 0.

We say that ff is strictly asymptotically convex if the previous inequality is strict.

Similarly, the reference measure μ\mu is (strictly) asymptotically log-concave if −log⁡μ-\log\mu is (strictly) asymptotically convex, underlying that μ\mu is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue and identifying μ\mu with its density. We notice that the class of asymptotically log-concave probability distributions encompasses Lipschitz-perturbations of log-concave measures.

The weak semiconvexity profile was introduced by [45] together with the probabilistic notion of coupling by reflection, and further used in [32] to establish exponential contraction for diffusion operators. More recently, the propagation of weak semiconvexity along generalized heat flows was systematically studied in [20], which further deduced many useful consequences – including building Lipschitz transport maps from the Gaussian towards strictly asymptotically log-concave measures [20, Theorem 1.4]. A partial analog of these results had been established in [7, Theorem 4.1] by PDE methods to prove the fundamental gap conjecture.

Exploiting the strict asymptotic log-concavity of the reference measure, a key result of the present article is the following extension of the Dacorogna-Moser construction to the entire ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Theorem 1.2 (Dacorogna-Moser construction on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Assume that μ\mu is a strictly asymptotically log-concave measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that ∇j​log​μ\nabla^{j}\log\mu is Lipschitz-continuous for every 1≤j≤n+11\leq j\leq n+1, n≥1n\geq 1. Let φ∈Wn,∞​(ℝd,ℝ)\varphi\in W^{n,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}) be such that ∫ℝdφ​𝑑μ=0\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\varphi\mathrm{d}\mu=0, ∥φ∥Wn,∞≤M\lVert\varphi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}}\leq M and φ≥−1+δ\varphi\geq-1+\delta, for some M,δ>0M,\delta>0. Then, there exists an invertible T:ℝd→ℝdT:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} such that (1+φ)⋅μ=T#​μ(1+\varphi)\cdot\mu=T_{\#}\mu, T−Id,T−1−Id∈Wn,∞​(ℝd,ℝd)T-\mathrm{Id},\ T^{-1}-\mathrm{Id}\in W^{n,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{d}) and

∥T−Id∥Wn,∞+∥T−1−Id∥Wn,∞≤C​∥φ∥Wn,∞,\lVert T-\mathrm{Id}\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}}+\lVert T^{-1}-\mathrm{Id}\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}}\leq C\lVert\varphi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}},

where C>0C>0 only depends on the bounds on log⁡μ\log\mu, the weak semiconvexity profile κ−log⁡μ,n\kappa_{-\log\mu},\ n and the constants MM, δ\delta.

A key feature of the above result is that the regularity bounds satisfied by TT are global in space. The proof can be found in Subsection 3.1. This result leverages the estimates on the PDE (3) that are proved in Proposition 2.1. In particular, we prove that the unique solution ψ∈H1​(μ)\psi\in H^{1}(\mu) of (3) satisfies ∥∇ψ∥Wn,∞≤C​∥φ∥Wn,∞\lVert\nabla\psi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}}\leq C\lVert\varphi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}}. This bound further relies on short- and long-time regularization estimates for the semi-group generated by the operator ∇logμ⋅∇+Δ\nabla\log\mu\cdot\nabla+\Delta, see Proposition 2.1.

Remark 1.3 (Additional regularity).

Comparing to the original Dacorogna-Moser result [28, Theorem 1], we would expect TT to have one more bounded derivative than φ\varphi. The Schauder regularity theory indeed provides local bounds for second-order derivatives of solutions of elliptic equations, which could be leveraged to prove additional local regularity for TT. On the contrary, the elliptic regularity estimate proved in Proposition 2.1 is global, as well as the result of Theorem 1.2, which is a key consequence of the asymptotic log-concavity of μ\mu. We do not expect higher-order global uniform estimates to be true in general – except for fractional regularity.

Since [28], the original Dacorogna-Moser construction has been used in many important works including Brenier’s variational model for incompressible fluids [16], where it plays a key role in building competitors to perform calculus of variation arguments. Adapting the approach from [16], a key application of Theorem 1.2 is to compute variations and derive optimality conditions for the problem of geodesics in the space of couplings of probability measures, which we introduce below, the precise statements of our results being presented later in Section 2.2. Once again, a key assumption will be the strict asymptotic log-concavity of the coupled marginals μ\mu and ν\nu.

1.1 Geodesics in the space of couplings

Let us fix μ,ν\mu,\nu in the Wasserstein space 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) of probability measures with finite second moment. Let us further consider ρ0,ρ1∈𝒫2​(ℝd×ℝd)\rho_{0},\rho_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}). Recalling the Benamou-Brenier formula [12], the Wasserstein distance between ρ0\rho_{0} and ρ1\rho_{1} can be written as

𝒲22(ρ0,ρ1)=inf{∫0112∥vt∥L2​(ρt)2dt:∂tρ+∇⋅(ρv)=0,(ρ|t=0,ρ|t=1)=(ρ0,ρ1)},\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})=\inf\bigg\{\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}\|v_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{t})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t:\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)=0,\,(\rho|_{t=0},\rho|_{t=1})=(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})\bigg\}, (5)

the continuity equation being understood in the weak sense and the factor 12\frac{1}{2} being here for later convenience. This formula allows for viewing 𝒫2​(ℝd×ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}) as a formal infinite-dimensional Riemannian manifold, as developed in [54].

Let us now assume that ρ0,ρ1\rho_{0},\rho_{1} belong to the sub-space Π⁡(μ,ν)⊂𝒫2​(ℝd×ℝd)\Pi(\mu,\nu)\subset\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}) of measures with first marginal μ\mu and second marginal ν\nu. If we restrict the minimization (5) to curves that stay in Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) at all times, then we get a formal notion of submanifold distance on Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) given by

dΠ⁡(μ,ν)2(ρ0,ρ1)=inf{∫0112∥vt∥L2​(ρt)2dt:∂tρ+∇⋅(ρv)=0,(ρ|t=0,ρ|t=1)=(ρ0,ρ1),ρt∈Π(μ,ν)}.d_{\Pi(\mu,\nu)}^{2}(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})=\inf\bigg\{\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}\|v_{t}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{t})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t:\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)=0,\ (\rho|_{t=0},\rho|_{t=1})=(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}),\rho_{t}\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\bigg\}. (6)

We say that (ρt)t∈[0,1](\rho_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} is a geodesic in Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) between ρ0\rho_{0} and ρ1\rho_{1} if it is a minimizer in (6).

The problem of geodesics in the space of couplings was first introduced in [26, Section 2.6], which was motivated by the construction of gradient flows in the induced geometry of Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu). In particular, [26] constructed dynamics that converge exponentially fast to the unique solution of the Schrödinger problem between μ\mu and ν\nu, while staying in Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) at every time when started from there. Although the long-time behavior of these dynamics shares some similarities with gradient flows in (Π⁡(μ,ν),dΠ⁡(μ,ν))(\Pi(\mu,\nu),d_{\Pi(\mu,\nu)}), they do not satisfy the rigorous requirements for being gradient flows. A major difficulty to build gradient flows is indeed the lack of geodesic convexity of Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) observed in [26, Proposition 2.2], so that the standard theory of gradient flows [5] – which usually requires geodesic convexity for the functional generating the flow – cannot be directly applied. This motivated the open question [26, Open Problem 6] of describing geodesics in Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu). The existence of geodesics was studied in [21, Proposition 3.1, Proposition 3.6] under the assumption that μ\mu, ν\nu are strongly log-concave and that log⁡μ\log\mu, log⁡ν\log\nu have bounded Hessian. In Section 2.2 below, we extend this existence result to marginals that are merely strictly asymptotically log-concave, before giving a complete PDE description of the geodesics answering [26, Open Problem 6].

By studying the optimality conditions for (6), we prove in Theorem 2.9 existence for Lagrange multipliers α\alpha and β\beta associated to the marginal constraints, which formally satisfy

{∂tρ+∇⋅(ρ∇φ)=0α⊕β=∂tφ+12​|∇φ|2,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho\nabla\varphi)=0\\ \alpha\oplus\beta=\partial_{t}\varphi+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\varphi|^{2},\end{cases} (7)

where φ\varphi is a multiplier associated to the continuity equation. Differentiating the second equation and combining it with the first one, we can formally write the conservation of momentum

ρ∇(α⊕β)=∂t(ρ∇φ)+∇⋅(ρ(∇φ⊗∇φ)).\rho\nabla(\alpha\oplus\beta)=\partial_{t}(\rho\nabla\varphi)+\nabla\cdot(\rho(\nabla\varphi\otimes\nabla\varphi)). (8)

The above computations are only formal, as we assumed existence and smoothness for the Lagrange multipliers α\alpha and β\beta, which does not hold in general. Under strict asymptotic log-concavity and regularity assumptions on the marginals, Theorem 2.9 below gives a rigorous meaning to α\alpha and β\beta as elements in the dual of some suitable functional spaces, which are rigorously defined in Definition 2.8. Under additional regularity assumptions, Theorem 2.11 then gives a rigorous meaning to the optimality conditions (8) for α\alpha and β\beta, deducing uniqueness for the multipliers at the same time. These results rely on calculus of variation arguments that crucially leverage our extended Dacorogna-Moser construction Theorem 1.2 to build competitors, similarly to how Brenier’s work [16] used the original bounded-domain Dacorogna-Moser construction.

The geometric structure of this problem is reminiscent of Brenier’s multiphase formulation of Euler’s incompressible equations [15, 16], which is itself a relaxation of Arnold’s formulation [8] of Euler’s equations for incompressible fluids. We recall that Arnold’s variational problem is given by

inf(Xt)t∈[0,1]∫01∫𝕋d12​|X˙t​(a)|2​𝑑a​𝑑t,\inf_{(X_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\frac{1}{2}|\dot{X}_{t}(a)|^{2}\mathrm{d}a\mathrm{d}t,

where the infimum is taken over absolutely continuous curves of diffeomorphisms Xt:𝕋d→𝕋dX_{t}:\mathbb{T}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{T}^{d} of the torus that preserve orientation and the Lebesgue measure (incompressibility constraint) at any time, with fixed endpoints at t=0t=0 and t=1t=1. A pressure field can then be introduced as a Lagrange multiplier for the incompressibility constraint, and the formal optimality conditions then correspond to a Lagrangian formulation of Euler’s equations. This problem is by now known as incompressible optimal transport, and we refer to [4, 29] for lecture notes on these variational models as well as to the textbook [18, Chapters 2-4].

Arnold’s problem is notoriously difficult as minimization is performed over a set that is not closed nor convex, and a minimizer does not exist in general [59, 60]. Therefore, [16] introduced the convex multiphase relaxation

inf(ρa,va)a∈𝕋d{∫𝕋d∫01∫𝕋d12|vta|2dρtadtda,∫𝕋dρtada=ℒ𝕋d∀t∈[0,1]},\inf_{(\rho^{a},v^{a})_{a\in\mathbb{T}^{d}}}\bigg\{\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\frac{1}{2}|v^{a}_{t}|^{2}\mathrm{d}\rho^{a}_{t}\mathrm{d}t\mathrm{d}a,\;\ \int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\rho_{t}^{a}\mathrm{d}a=\mathcal{L}_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\ \forall t\in[0,1]\bigg\}, (9)

where (ρa,va)(\rho^{a},v^{a}) satisfies the continuity equation for almost every a∈𝕋da\in\mathbb{T}^{d}, ℒ𝕋d\mathcal{L}_{\mathbb{T}^{d}} is the Lebesgue measure on 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d} and the endpoints at t=0t=0 and t=1t=1 are fixed. Similarly, a pressure field can be introduced as a Lagrange multiplier for the incompressibility constraint, whose properties are further detailed in Section 1.2 below.

Motivated by the classical entropic regularization of optimal transport and its connection with the Schrödinger bridge problem [44], [48] introduced an analogous regularization of Brenier’s incompressible optimal transport, which is known as the Brödinger problem – in particular, this regularization restores uniqueness for the minimizer and can be seen as the Schrödinger bridge problem on the space of couplings; we refer the reader to Section 2.2 and Appendix A for a detailed presentation.

Exploiting the similarity between the constrained minimization problems (6) and (9), we introduce an analog regularization for (6) in Section 2.2, which we study by adapting the methods developed in [11, 9] for the Brödinger problem. As for the Brödinger problem, we could have studied an entropic pathwise formulation, which we mention in the Appendix. We thus prove existence and uniqueness for Lagrange multipliers in both regularized and un-regularized settings, and we derive the related optimality conditions. The precise connection between the regularization and the original geodesic problem is given by a Γ\Gamma-convergence result in Theorem 2.6, as well as weak-⋆\star convergence for the multipliers in Proposition 2.12.

1.2 Literature review

Hereafter, we review several contributions related to problems discussed in this article.

Transport maps on bounded domains.

As previously mentioned, [28] showed a way to construct regular transport maps between two probability distributions that are supported on bounded sets. More precisely, given a bounded set Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with a Ck+3,αC^{k+3,\alpha} boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, for some integer k≥0k\geq 0, α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), and functions f,g∈Ck,α​(Ω¯)f,g\in C^{k,\alpha}(\overline{\Omega}) such that f,g>0f,g>0 on Ω¯\overline{\Omega} and ∫f​𝑑x=∫g​𝑑x\int f\mathrm{d}x=\int g\mathrm{d}x, [28, Theorem 1] constructs a transport map TT from f​d​xf\mathrm{d}x to g​d​xg\mathrm{d}x that fixes the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, and such that T,T−1∈Ck+1,α​(Ω¯,ℝd)T,T^{-1}\in C^{k+1,\alpha}(\overline{\Omega},\mathbb{R}^{d}). This result was later improved by relaxing the Hölder-continuity of densities in [56, Theorem 1, Theorem 2], allowing for weaker conditions such as bounded or BMO densities. [56, Section 3] is based on a flow-map construction analogous to [28], but using convolution as a regularizing interpolation instead of linear interpolation – this method could work on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} as well. On the contrary, the proof of Theorem 1.2 below uses the linear interpolation of [28] without regularization. Recalling Remark 1.3, we emphasize that the bound on TT in Theorem 1.2 has one less degree of regularity than in the aforementioned works; however, the key feature of Theorem 1.2 is to prove global regularity estimates on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, contrary to these works.

In the recent literature, several strategies have been proposed to build transport maps on the whole ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, one popular method relying on the time-reversal of diffusion processes.

Time-reversed diffusion and Langevin dynamics.

[42, Theorem 1.1] constructed a 1-Lipschitz transport map from μ⁡(d​x)=e−U⁡(x)​d​x\mu(\mathrm{d}x)=e^{-U(x)}\mathrm{d}x to a measure ν=e−V⁡(x)​μ​(d​x)\nu=e^{-V(x)}\mu(\mathrm{d}x), where VV is convex and U∈Cl​o​c3,α​(ℝd)U\in C^{3,\alpha}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), α>0\alpha>0, is a convex function with a specific shape that makes it sufficiently coercive. The construction relies on the generalized heat flow

∂tμt=Δ​μt−∇U⋅∇μt+Δ​U​μt,μ0=ν,\partial_{t}\mu_{t}=\Delta\mu_{t}-\nabla U\cdot\nabla\mu_{t}+\Delta U\mu_{t},\quad\mu_{0}=\nu,

whose solution converges towards μ\mu as t→+∞t\to+\infty. Equivalently, μt\mu_{t} is the law at time tt of the overdamped Langevin dynamics

d​Xt=−∇U​(Xt)​d​t+2​d​Bt,X0∼ν,\mathrm{d}X_{t}=-\nabla U(X_{t})\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\mathrm{d}B_{t},\quad X_{0}\sim\nu, (10)

driven by a Brownian motion (Bt)t≥0(B_{t})_{t\geq 0}. Introducing the flow maps St:ℝd→ℝdS_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying

dd​tSt=−∇logd​μtd​μ∘St,S0=Id,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}S_{t}=-\nabla\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\circ S_{t},\quad S_{0}=\text{Id}, (11)

we have St→S∞S_{t}\rightarrow S_{\infty} as t→+∞t\rightarrow+\infty with μt=(St)#​ν\mu_{t}=(S_{t})_{\#}\nu, so that the desired Lipschitz transport map from μ\mu to ν\nu – or heat flow map – is given by T:=S∞−1T:=S_{\infty}^{-1}. We notice that the quantity vt:=−∇log⁡(μt/μ)v_{t}:=-\nabla\log(\mu_{t}/\mu) in (11) defines a vector field such that (μt,vt)t∈[0,1](\mu_{t},v_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} satisfies the continuity equation. [42, Theorem 1.1] then proves that TT is a contraction, similarly to Caffarelli’s result for the optimal transport map [19]. This construction was later leveraged to build Lipschitz transport maps under different assumptions.

The Langevin diffusion (10) has been further used in [34, Theorem 1] to show existence for a bi-Lipschitz transport map from an α\alpha-log concave measure μ=e−U\mu=e^{-U}, α>0\alpha>0, to any log-Lipschitz perturbation ν=e−U+V\nu=e^{-U+V}, i.e. VV is Lipschitz-continuous, under an additional boundedness assumption on ∇3U\nabla^{3}U. An extension to manifold settings was further proposed by [47].

Our extended Dacorogna-Moser construction also leverages the regularization and contraction properties of the Langevin diffusion (10) to prove PDE estimates in Proposition 2.1. Regarding assumptions, we relax the strong log-concavity assumption on μ\mu into the less restrictive requirement that μ\mu is strictly asymptotically log-concave. However, our regularity assumptions are slightly stronger, as we require both ∇U\nabla U and ∇2U\nabla^{2}U to be Lipschitz – see Assumption (A.1) below. We also need to assume that the log-perturbation VV is bounded and Lipschitz-continuous (φ=eV−1\varphi=e^{V}-1 in our notation), whereas [34, Theorem 1] only requires VV being Lipschitz. This is related to the fact that we consider target measures of the shape (1+φ)⋅μ(1+\varphi)\cdot\mu, and we control the Lipschitz constant directly in terms of φ\varphi, as it is more suitable for the geodesic problem studied in Section 2.2. We furthermore quantify the higher-order regularity of the transport map in terms of the one of φ\varphi.

Gaussian setting and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diffusion.

Various improvements have been proposed for the case where μ\mu is the standard Gaussian, i.e. U⁡(x)=12​|x|2U(x)=\frac{1}{2}|x|^{2}. [51, Theorem 1, Theorem 2] proves the Lipschitz-continuity of the heat flow map when the target measure ν\nu is strongly log-concave, or when ν\nu is the convolution of the standard Gaussian with a compactly supported measure. To do so, [51, Lemma 3] establishes an explicit bound on the Lipschitz constant, which depends on the derivative of the velocity field in (11) – also called the score function – thus reducing the problem to bounding −∇2​log​(μt/μ)-\nabla^{2}\log(\mu_{t}/\mu). This estimate is exploited in [20, Theorem 1.4] to prove existence for a Lipschitz map from the standard Gaussian to any strictly asymptotically log-concave measure ν\nu such that ∫01r​κ−log⁡ν−​(r)​𝑑r<+∞\int_{0}^{1}r\kappa^{-}_{-\log\nu}(r)\mathrm{d}r<+\infty, recalling the definition (4) of the weak semiconvexity profile.

More generally, proving Lipschitz bounds on the score function for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process has become a common strategy, which is used in [40, Theorem 1] to prove existence of bi-Lipschitz transport maps from the standard Gaussian to a general class of measures, which includes Gaussian mixtures and convolutions of Gaussians with compactly supported measures. Similarly, by studying the regularity of the score function, [62, Theorem 2] proves that the heat flow map belongs to C⌊β⌋+1C^{\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1} when the target measure ν\nu is a bounded β\beta-Hölder perturbation of the standard Gaussian, allowing for quantifying the regularity of the map depending on the one of the perturbation.

Our results in Theorem 1.2 are less precise than the aforementioned ones on Hölder-perturbations of Gaussians, but our setting is more general as it allows for any initial distribution μ\mu that is strictly asymptotically log-concave – not necessarily a Gaussian. For the sake of completeness, we finally mention the works [24, 23], which prove quantitative stability for the heat-flow map with respect to the target distribution ν\nu, in the Gaussian case.

Other interpolations.

Many other methods to construct transport maps have been proposed in the recent literature. A famous strategy introduced by [46] is flow matching, which amounts to using the flows of probability measures and vector fields given by

μt​(x)=∫μt​(x|x1)​𝑑ν​(x1),vt​(x)=∫vt​(x|x1)​μt​(x|x1)μt​(x)​𝑑ν​(x1),\mu_{t}(x)=\int\mu_{t}(x|x_{1})\mathrm{d}\nu(x_{1}),\qquad v_{t}(x)=\int v_{t}(x|x_{1})\frac{\mu_{t}(x|x_{1})}{\mu_{t}(x)}\mathrm{d}\nu(x_{1}),

where ν\nu is the target distribution, μt​(x|x1)\mu_{t}(x|x_{1}) is a conditional distribution such that μ0​(x|x1)=μ⁡(x)\mu_{0}(x|x_{1})=\mu(x) – so that μ0=μ\mu_{0}=\mu – and μ1​(x|x1)\mu_{1}(x|x_{1}) is concentrated around x1x_{1} – so that μ1\mu_{1} approximates ν\nu. A possible choice of conditional measure is the Gaussian

μt​(x|x1)=𝒩⁡(x|mt​(x1),σt2​(x1)​Id),\mu_{t}(x|x_{1})=\mathcal{N}(x|m_{t}(x_{1}),\sigma_{t}^{2}(x_{1})I_{d}),

for some suitable choice of the conditional mean mtm_{t} and variance σt2\sigma^{2}_{t}. If σt\sigma_{t} only depends on time for simplicity, σ0=1=1−σ1\sigma_{0}=1=1-\sigma_{1} and mt​(x1)=t​x1m_{t}(x_{1})=tx_{1}, then μt\mu_{t} corresponds to the law at time tt of the stochastic process

Xt=mt​(Y)+σt​ξ,Y∼ν,ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),X_{t}=m_{t}(Y)+\sigma_{t}\xi,\quad Y\sim\nu,\quad\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}),

so that (Xt)t∈[0,1](X_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} is a stochastic interpolation between the initial Gaussian distribution and the target measure. This construction can be extended to other stochastic interpolants between arbitrary distributions, as in [2] that studies the laws of the process

Xt=mt​(X0,Y),Y∼ν,X0∼μ,X_{t}=m_{t}(X_{0},Y),\quad Y\sim\nu,\quad X_{0}\sim\mu,

and further generalized in [1] as

Xt=mt​(X0,Y)+σt​ξ,ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,Id).X_{t}=m_{t}(X_{0},Y)+\sigma_{t}\xi,\quad\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}).

For different choices of mtm_{t} and σt\sigma_{t}, [63] proves dimension-free bounds for the Lipschitz constant of the resulting transport map from the standard Gaussian to a target measure of the form e−V⁡(x)+W⁡(x)​d​xe^{-V(x)+W(x)}\mathrm{d}x, where V∈C2​(ℝd,ℝ)V\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}) is α\alpha-convex, α>0\alpha>0, and WW is β\beta-Hölder, β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1]. In particular, [63, Corollary 1] covers the Lipman flow matching setting, and [63, Corollary 2] considers the stochastic-interpolant flow matching setting. Furthermore, the aforementioned Ornstein-Uhlenbeck setting can be seen as a specific instance of this type of interpolation for mt​(x,y)=t​ym_{t}(x,y)=ty and σt=1−t2\sigma_{t}=\sqrt{1-t^{2}}, and the Lipschitz-continuity of the resulting transport map is proved in [63, Corollary 3]. The target measure is strictly asymptotically log-concave when β=1\beta=1, and this result overlaps [20, Theorem 1.4] in this case. For a general value β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), neither of these two results implies the other one.

Once again, we emphasize that this setting is different from ours, as the starting measure μ\mu in Theorem 1.2 needs not be a Gaussian, and we study the regularity of the Dacorogna-Moser transport map with respect to the one of the perturbation φ\varphi in the target measure (1+φ)⋅μ(1+\varphi)\cdot\mu.

Geodesics in the space of couplings.

The basic references [26, 21] on the geodesic problem in Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) have already been discussed in Section 1.1. We therefore focus here on related variational problems that motivate our analysis.

Our study of Lagrange multipliers is inspired by Brenier’s multiphase formulation of incompressible Euler equations [16]. In that setting, the pressure arises as the Lagrange multiplier associated with the incompressibility constraint and is shown to be unique as a distribution, with ∇p∈ℳ⁡((0,1)×𝕋d)\nabla p\in\mathcal{M}((0,1)\times\mathbb{T}^{d}). The regularity theory was subsequently refined in [35], which proves that ∇p∈L2​((0,1),ℳ⁡(𝕋d))\nabla p\in L^{2}((0,1),\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{T}^{d})) and p∈L2​((0,1),Ld/(d−1)​(𝕋d))p\in L^{2}((0,1),L^{d/(d-1)}(\mathbb{T}^{d})). Determining the optimal regularity of the pressure remains a challenging open question, see for instance the semiconcavity conjecture in [17]. In contrast, our work establishes existence, uniqueness, and rigorous optimality conditions for the Lagrange multipliers associated with the marginal constraints, but does not address their optimal regularity. Whether or not the techniques of [35] can be adapted to our setting is an interesting open question.

The regularized problem considered in this article is similarly motivated by the entropic regularization of Brenier’s formulation. This latter regularization was introduced in [48] as the Brödinger problem; it amounts to adding a Fisher-information term to the kinetic energy – see Appendix A. In particular, this regularization restores uniqueness of the minimizer, which does not hold in general for the unregularized Brenier problem. Building on this formulation, [11] establishes existence, uniqueness, and optimality conditions for the pressure field, while [9] proves Γ\Gamma-convergence towards Brenier’s multiphase problem together with weak-⋆\star convergence of the associated multipliers.

Our approach follows the same general strategy, but substantial modifications are required. In particular, the heat-flow regularization used in [9] does not preserve the constraint set Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) and therefore cannot be used to construct recovery sequences. Instead, assuming that ∇2​log​μ\nabla^{2}\log\mu and ∇2​log​ν\nabla^{2}\log\nu are bounded, we regularize by the gradient flow of the relative entropy H(⋅∣μ⊗ν)H(\cdot\mid\mu\otimes\nu) in (𝒫2​(ℝd×ℝd),𝒲2)(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}),\mathcal{W}_{2}), which leaves Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) invariant. The required regularization estimates are obtained using the theory of the Schrödinger bridge problem on general metric spaces developed in [52].

2 Statement of the main results

In this section, we state our main results on the extended Dacorogna-Moser construction and the geodesic problem.

2.1 The extended Dacorogna-Moser construction

Our main result Theorem 1.2 requires the following assumption.

Assumption (A.1).

  1. (i)

    μ\mu is strictly asymptotically log-concave – see Definition 1.1;

  2. (ii)

    ∇j​log​μ\nabla^{j}\log\mu is well-defined and Lipschitz-continuous for every j∈{1,…,n+1}j\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\} for some n≥0n\geq 0.

As mentioned in Section 1, the transport map in Theorem 1.2 is constructed from a flow of probability measures (ρs)s∈[0,1](\rho_{s})_{s\in[0,1]} between μ\mu and (1+φ)⋅μ(1+\varphi)\cdot\mu, for a suitable choice of velocity vector field (vs)s∈[0,1](v_{s})_{s\in[0,1]} such that the continuity equation (1) is satisfied. The transport map is then given by the flow generated by the velocity at the terminal time. The simplifying assumptions ρs=(1+s​φ)⋅μ\rho_{s}=(1+s\varphi)\cdot\mu and vs=−∇ψ1+s​φv_{s}=-\frac{\nabla\psi}{1+s\varphi} reduce the continuity equation to solving the equation Δμ​ψ=φ\Delta_{\mu}\psi=\varphi – recalling the Δμ\Delta_{\mu} notation introduced in Section 1.3. Therefore, the desired estimates on the transport map in Theorem 1.2 result from estimating the solution of this equation. This is the content of the following result, whose proof can be found in Section 3.1. For convenience in writing the proof, the result is stated for the operator 12​Δμ\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\mu} rather than Δμ\Delta_{\mu}, but the resulting estimates are equivalent.

Proposition 2.1 (Parabolic and elliptic PDE estimates).

Let μ\mu be a probability measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} that satisfies Assumption (A.1) for some n≥0n\geq 0, and let φ∈Wn,∞​(ℝd,ℝ)\varphi\in W^{n,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}) be such that ∫ℝdφ​𝑑μ=0\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\varphi\mathrm{d}\mu=0. Let (St)t≥0(S_{t})_{t\geq 0} be the semigroup generated by the operator 12​Δμ\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\mu} defined in Section 1.3. Then:

  1. (i)

    ∇Stφ∈Wn,∞\nabla S_{t}\varphi\in W^{n,\infty} for every t>0t>0, and there exist constants c,α>0c,\alpha>0 that only depend on μ\mu and nn such that

    {∥∇Stφ∥Wn,∞≤ce−α​t∥φ∥Wn,∞,∀t≥1,∥∇Stφ∥Wn,∞≤ct∥φ∥Wn,∞,∀t∈(0,1].\begin{cases}\lVert\nabla S_{t}\varphi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}}\leq ce^{-\alpha t}\lVert\varphi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}},\quad\forall t\geq 1,\\ \lVert\nabla S_{t}\varphi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}}\leq\frac{c}{\sqrt{t}}\lVert\varphi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}},\quad\forall t\in(0,1].\end{cases} (12)
  2. (ii)

    The system

    12​Δμ​ψ=φ,∫ℝdψ​𝑑μ=0,\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\mu}\psi=\varphi,\qquad\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi\mathrm{d}\mu=0, (13)

    admits a unique solution ψ∈H1​(μ)\psi\in H^{1}(\mu), which is given by ψ=−∫0+∞Stφdt\psi=-\int_{0}^{+\infty}S_{t}\varphi\mathrm{d}t. Furthermore, ∇ψ∈Wn,∞\nabla\psi\in W^{n,\infty} and

    ∥∇ψ∥Wn,∞≤C​∥φ∥Wn,∞,\lVert\nabla\psi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}}\leq C\lVert\varphi\rVert_{W^{n,\infty}}, (14)

    where C>0C>0 is a constant that only depends on μ\mu and nn.

Remark 2.2 (Explicit constants).

The constants that appear in the estimates (12)-(14) can be made explicit, even though their expression is quite heavy – see [31, Theorem 1] and [55, Theorem 3.4]. These expressions depend on the weak log-concavity profile κ−log⁡μ\kappa_{-\log\mu} of the reference measure.

The proof of (12) relies on the Feynman-Kac stochastic representation formula and coupling by reflection, leveraging the estimates proved in [55] and [31]. The bound (14) follows, as we can verify that the solution is formally given by ψ=−∫0∞Stφdt\psi=-\int_{0}^{\infty}S_{t}\varphi\mathrm{d}t and then leverage the estimates on St​φS_{t}\varphi.

Remark 2.3 (Regularity of the profile).

To apply the estimates [31, Theorem 1] and [55, Theorem 3.4], we also need to assume

∫01r​κ−log⁡μ−​(r)​𝑑r<+∞,\int_{0}^{1}r\kappa_{-\log\mu}^{-}(r)\mathrm{d}r<+\infty,

but this is implied by (ii) in (A.1), because ∇log⁡μ\nabla\log\mu is Lipschitz-continuous.

2.2 The geodesic problem and its regularization

In this section, we state our main results about the geodesic problem, the proofs being deferred to Section 3.2. First, we introduce a regularization of the geodesic problem using the relative Fisher information, taking inspiration from the regularization of Brenier’s multiphase formulation of incompressible fluids given by the Brödinger’s problem [48].

Definition 2.4 (The regularized problem).

Let ρ0,ρ1∈Π⁡(μ,ν)\rho_{0},\rho_{1}\in\Pi(\mu,\nu). For every ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in[0,1], we define

𝒜ε(ρ):=inf{12∫01∫ℝd×ℝd|vt|2dρtdt+ε28∫01∫ℝd×ℝd|∇logd​ρtd​μ⊗ν|2dρtdt,∂tρ+∇⋅(ρv)=0},\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon}(\rho):=\inf\bigg\{\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}|v_{t}|^{2}\mathrm{d}\rho_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{8}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\bigg\lvert\nabla\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\rho_{t}}{\mathrm{d}\mu\otimes\nu}\bigg\rvert^{2}\mathrm{d}\rho_{t}\mathrm{d}t,\ \partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)=0\bigg\},

and we consider the minimization problem

inf{𝒜ε​(ρ),(ρt)t∈[0,1]⊂Π⁡(μ,ν),(ρ|t=0,ρ|t=1)=(ρ0,ρ1)}.\inf\big\{\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon}(\rho),(\rho_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}\subset\Pi(\mu,\nu),(\rho|_{t=0},\rho|_{t=1})=(\rho_{0},\rho_{1})\big\}. (15)

We refer to Appendix A for an alternative formulation motivating this regularized problem, which can be seen as the Schrödinger bridge problem on the space of couplings.

Remark 2.5 (Geodesic problem).

When ε=0\varepsilon=0, the minimization problem (15) is the geodesic problem (6).

For both the geodesic problem and its regularization (15), we prove finiteness and existence of minimizers, and we show convergence as ε\varepsilon tends to zero. In particular, the following result establishes existence of geodesics in the strict asymptotic log-concavity setting and proves Γ\Gamma-convergence of the regularized problem (15) towards the geodesic problem.

Theorem 2.6 (Existence of geodesics and Γ\Gamma-convergence).

Suppose that μ\mu and ν\nu satisfy Assumption (A.1) for n=0n=0, and let ρ0,ρ1∈Π⁡(μ,ν)\rho_{0},\rho_{1}\in\Pi(\mu,\nu). Then, the problem (15) with ε=0\varepsilon=0 admits at least one minimizer. Furthermore, assuming that H⁡(ρ0|μ⊗ν),H⁡(ρ1|μ⊗ν)<+∞H(\rho_{0}|\mu\otimes\nu),H(\rho_{1}|\mu\otimes\nu)<+\infty, then for every ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1] the minimization problem (15) is finite, it admits a unique minimizer and

Γ−limε→0𝒜ε+i01=𝒜0+i01,\Gamma-\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon}+i_{01}=\mathcal{A}_{0}+i_{01},

for the uniform convergence in C⁡([0,1],Π⁡(μ,ν))C([0,1],\Pi(\mu,\nu)) and for the pointwise-in-time convergence with respect to the topology of weak convergence of measures on Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu), where i01​(γ)=0i_{01}(\gamma)=0 if (γ0,γ1)=(ρ0,ρ1)(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1})=(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}) and i01​(γ)=+∞i_{01}(\gamma)=+\infty otherwise.

Existence of minimizers is ensured by [21] in the strong log-concavity setting, and we extend this result to the general case using a Lipschitz-continuous transport map from the standard Gaussian to any strictly asymptotically log-concave measure [20, Theorem 1.4]. The Γ\Gamma-convergence proof leverages estimates contained in [52] for the Schrödinger problem on general metric spaces.

Remark 2.7 (Sufficient assumption).

The only properties needed for the proof of Theorem 2.6 are the existence of Lipschitz-continuous transport maps from the standard Gaussian distribution to the marginals μ\mu and ν\nu, and the fact that ∇2​log​μ\nabla^{2}\log\mu and ∇2​log​ν\nabla^{2}\log\nu are bounded.

To better understand the structure of geodesics and minimizers of the regularized problem, we are interested in deriving optimality conditions. To do so, we show existence of a Lagrange multiplier associated to the marginal constraints, and we then derive rigorous optimality conditions. This first requires defining the appropriate notion of perturbation.

Definition 2.8 (Space of perturbations and modified problem).

We define the space SμS_{\mu} of functions φ:[0,1]×ℝd→ℝ\varphi:[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} that satisfy, writing φ=(φt)t∈[0,1]\varphi=(\varphi_{t})_{t\in[0,1]},

φ0≡φ1≡0,∫ℝdφ​𝑑μ=0,\displaystyle\varphi_{0}\equiv\varphi_{1}\equiv 0,\qquad\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\varphi\mathrm{d}\mu=0,
φ∈L∞​([0,1],W2,∞​(ℝd))∩W1,2​((0,1),L∞​(ℝd)).\displaystyle\varphi\in L^{\infty}([0,1],W^{2,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))\cap W^{1,2}((0,1),L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})).

We similarly define the space SνS_{\nu} and we equip both spaces with the norm

N⁡(φ):=ess​supt∈[0,1]⁡∥φt∥W2,∞​(ℝd)+(∫01∥∂tφt∥L∞​(ℝd)2​dt)1/2.N(\varphi):=\esssup_{t\in[0,1]}\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{W^{2,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}+\bigg(\int_{0}^{1}\lVert\partial_{t}\varphi_{t}\rVert^{2}_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{1/2}.

For every (μt)t∈[0,1],(νt)t∈[0,1]∈C⁡([0,1],𝒫2​(ℝd))(\mu_{t})_{t\in[0,1]},(\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}\in C([0,1],\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})) such that μ0=μ1=μ\mu_{0}=\mu_{1}=\mu and ν0=ν1=ν\nu_{0}=\nu_{1}=\nu, we define the functional

(16)

If μt=(1+φt)⋅μ\mu_{t}=(1+\varphi_{t})\cdot\mu, νt=(1+ψt)⋅ν\nu_{t}=(1+\psi_{t})\cdot\nu for φ∈Sμ,ψ∈Sν\varphi\in S_{\mu},\psi\in S_{\nu}, then we denote (16) by ℱε​(φ,ψ)\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(\varphi,\psi); if either 1+φ1+\varphi or 1+ψ1+\psi is not non-negative, then we set ℱε​(φ,ψ):=+∞\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(\varphi,\psi):=+\infty.

Using this notion of perturbation for the marginal constraints, we now establish existence of the Lagrange multiplier for both the geodesic problem and its regularization.

Theorem 2.9 (Existence of the Lagrange multiplier).

Suppose that μ\mu and ν\nu satisfy Assumption (A.1) with n=2n=2. Then for every ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in[0,1], there exists pεp^{\varepsilon} in the convex sub-differential ∂ℱε​(0,0)⊂(Sμ×Sν)′\partial\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(0,0)\subset(S_{\mu}\times S_{\nu})^{\prime} of ℱε\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon} at (0,0)(0,0), meaning that

ℱε​(φ,ψ)≥ℱε​(0,0)+⟨pε,(φ,ψ)⟩∀φ∈Sμ,ψ∈Sν.\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(\varphi,\psi)\geq\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(0,0)+\langle p^{\varepsilon},(\varphi,\psi)\rangle\quad\forall\varphi\in S_{\mu},\psi\in S_{\nu}. (17)

The proof shows that ℱε\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon} is bounded near the origin in Sμ×SνS_{\mu}\times S_{\nu}, and then deduces existence of an element in ∂ℱε​(0,0)\partial\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(0,0) by convexity and lower semicontinuity of ℱε\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}. The boundedness of ℱε​(φ,ψ)\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(\varphi,\psi) near the origin crucially relies on the extended Dacorogna-Moser construction from Theorem 1.2 to build transport maps from μ\mu and ν\nu to the perturbed marginals, before using them as competitors for the modified problem (16). We then leverage the estimates on these maps to bound ℱε​(φ,ψ)\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(\varphi,\psi).

Now knowing existence for Lagrange multipliers, we can perform a first-order expansion of the inequality (17) to derive optimality conditions. However, this expansion requires more regularity for the perturbations, motivating the following definition.

Definition 2.10 (Regular spaces of perturbations).

We say that φ\varphi belongs to the space S~μ\tilde{S}_{\mu} if φ∈Sμ\varphi\in S_{\mu} and φ∈L∞​([0,1],W3,∞​(ℝd))∩W1,2​([0,1],W1,∞​(ℝd))\varphi\in L^{\infty}([0,1],W^{3,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))\cap W^{1,2}([0,1],W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})), and we equip it with the same norm N⁡(⋅)N(\cdot) as the one on SμS_{\mu}. We similarly define the space S~ν\tilde{S}_{\nu}.

The following result now gives a rigorous meaning to the formal optimality conditions (7), and deduces uniqueness for the Lagrange multipliers of both the geodesic problem and its regularization on the space (S~μ×S~ν)′(\tilde{S}_{\mu}\times\tilde{S}_{\nu})^{\prime}.

Theorem 2.11 (Optimality conditions and uniqueness for the multipliers).

Suppose that μ\mu and ν\nu satisfy Assumption (A.1) with n=3n=3. For ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in[0,1], let (ρ,v)(\rho,v) be a minimizer for ℱε​(0,0)\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(0,0) and pε∈∂ℱε​(0,0)p^{\varepsilon}\in\partial\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(0,0). Then, for every φ∈S~μ\varphi\in\tilde{S}_{\mu} and ψ∈S~ν\psi\in\tilde{S}_{\nu}, we have

⟨pε,(φ,ψ)⟩=⟨∂t(ρ​v)+div⁡{(v⊗v−wε⊗wε)​ρ},(∇f,∇g)⟩\langle p^{\varepsilon},(\varphi,\psi)\rangle=\langle\partial_{t}(\rho v)+\operatorname{div}\{(v\otimes v-w^{\varepsilon}\otimes w^{\varepsilon})\rho\},(\nabla f,\nabla g)\rangle (18)

where

wε:=ε2∇logd​ρd​μ⊗ν,∀ε∈(0,1],w^{\varepsilon}:=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\rho}{\mathrm{d}\mu\otimes\nu},\quad\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1],

In particular, since (18) holds for every minimizer (ρ,v)(\rho,v), this implies uniqueness for pεp^{\varepsilon} in (S~μ×S~ν)′(\tilde{S}_{\mu}\times\tilde{S}_{\nu})^{\prime}, for every ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in[0,1].

Our derivation of optimality conditions is strongly inspired by [11]. In this work, the quantity wεw^{\varepsilon} is substituted by ε2∇logρ\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla\log\rho, and the marginal constraint is replaced by the incompressibility constraint, which corresponds to imposing the Lebesgue measure as one of the marginals. Moreover, [11, Lemma 14] proves optimality conditions for the distributional gradient of the pressure against C1,2C^{1,2} test functions, whereas the adequate space of test functions in our case is S~μ×S~ν\tilde{S}_{\mu}\times\tilde{S}_{\nu}, requiring test functions to have three derivatives with respect to space. This restriction is due to the fact that W3,∞​(ℝd)W^{3,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is not dense in W2,∞∩C2​(ℝd)W^{2,\infty}\cap C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) – whereas W3,∞​(𝕋d)W^{3,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}) is dense in C2​(𝕋d)C^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{d}) –, preventing us from extending (18) by density. For the same reason, our weak-⋆\star convergence result Proposition 2.12 for multipliers only holds in (S~μ×S~ν)′(\tilde{S}_{\mu}\times\tilde{S}_{\nu})^{\prime}, whereas the analog result for the Brödinger problem [9, Theorem 2.6] considers test functions in C1,2​([0,1]×𝕋d)C^{1,2}([0,1]\times\mathbb{T}^{d}). We state our weak-⋆\star convergence result hereafter.

Proposition 2.12 (Convergence of the Lagrange multipliers).

For every ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in[0,1], let pεp^{\varepsilon} be the unique element of ∂ℱε​(0,0)\partial\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}(0,0) in (S~μ×S~ν)′(\tilde{S}_{\mu}\times\tilde{S}_{\nu})^{\prime}. Then, for every φ∈S~μ\varphi\in\tilde{S}_{\mu} and ψ∈S~ν\psi\in\tilde{S}_{\nu}, we have

⟨pε,(φ,ψ)⟩→⟨p0,(φ,ψ)⟩.\langle p^{\varepsilon},(\varphi,\psi)\rangle\rightarrow\langle p^{0},(\varphi,\psi)\rangle. (19)

3 Proofs

This section is devoted to the proof of the results stated in Section 2.

3.2 The problem of geodesics in the space of couplings

Proof of the existence of geodesics and of Γ\Gamma-convergence (Theorem 2.6).

We first prove the existence of geodesics and then Γ\Gamma-convergence.

Existence of geodesics.

Assuming that μ\mu and ν\nu are λ\lambda-log-concave for some λ>0\lambda>0, the existence of geodesics is proved in [21, Section 3], recalling that ∇2​log​μ\nabla^{2}\log\mu and ∇2​log​ν\nabla^{2}\log\nu are bounded from Assumption (A.1). More specifically, [21, Proposition 3.6] proves existence of curves of finite length in Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) and uses the compactness criteria [21, Proposition 3.1] to deduce existence of geodesics – taking σ\sigma therein to be the topology of weak convergence of measures. The same argument provides existence of geodesics in the strictly asymptotically log-concave setting if we show existence of curves of finite length connecting any two points in Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu).

Using the strict asymptotic log-concavity of μ\mu, ν\nu and Remark 2.3, [20, Theorem 1.4] provides invertible transport maps TT and SS with finite Lipschitz constant L>0L>0 from the standard Gaussian γ\gamma on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} to μ\mu and ν\nu, respectively. Let ρ0\rho_{0}, ρ1\rho_{1} be any two points in Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu). We have that ηi:=(T−1,S−1)#​ρi∈Π⁡(γ,γ)\eta_{i}:=(T^{-1},S^{-1})_{\#}\rho_{i}\in\Pi(\gamma,\gamma) for i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}. From the aforementioned result in [21, Section 3], there exists an absolutely continuous curve of finite length (ηt)t∈[0,1]⊂Π⁡(γ,γ)(\eta_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}\subset\Pi(\gamma,\gamma) connecting η0\eta_{0} to η1\eta_{1}, and let (wt)t∈[0,1](w_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} be a velocity vector field provided by [5, Theorem 8.3.1] such that (η,w)(\eta,w) satisfies the continuity equation (1) and

𝒜0​(η)=∫01∫ℝd×ℝd12​|wt|2​d​ηt​𝑑t.\mathcal{A}_{0}(\eta)=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{2}|w_{t}|^{2}\mathrm{d}\eta_{t}\mathrm{d}t.

Defining

we can check that (ρ,v)(\rho,v) satisfies the continuity equation, and that ρt∈Π⁡(μ,ν)\rho_{t}\in\Pi(\mu,\nu) for every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. From |∇T|,|∇S|≤L|\nabla T|,|\nabla S|\leq L, we have

Finiteness of the regularized problem.

This part relies on estimates from [52], which studies a general minimization problem in metric measure spaces. Rather than providing an incomplete introduction to the theory of optimal transport and gradient flow in metric spaces, we refer the reader to the textbook [5] – or more concisely to the definitions provided in [52, Setting 3.1] and references therein.

where

Existence and uniqueness for the regularized problem.

The existence of a minimizer is a direct adaptation of [21, Proposition 3.1], using compactness for a sequence of minimizing curves and lower semicontinuity with respect to the weak convergence of measures. The lower semicontinuity of the objective function follows from the one of 𝒜0​(ρ)\mathcal{A}_{0}(\rho) – see e.g. [6, Section 2.2] – and the one of the remaining term, using Fatou’s lemma and the lower semicontinuity of |∂H(⋅|μ⊗ν)|2|\partial H(\cdot|\mu\otimes\nu)|^{2} – proved in [5, Theorem 10.4.14]. The uniqueness of the minimizer for ε>0\varepsilon>0 is a consequence of the strict convexity of the Fisher information on the set of positive probability measures, combined with the usual convexity of the kinetic action with respect to (ρ,ρ​v)(\rho,\rho v) for (ρ,v)(\rho,v) satisfying the continuity equation (1).

𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-convergence.

Similarly, it is sufficient to prove the lim sup\limsup inequality with respect to the dΠ⁡(μ,ν)d_{\Pi(\mu,\nu)}-uniform one. Proposition 3.1 (Convexity and lower semicontinuity of ℱε\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon}).

For every ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in[0,1] the functional ℱε\mathcal{F}_{\varepsilon} is convex and lower semicontinuous with respect to the topology on C​([0,1],𝒫2​(ℝd))2C([0,1],\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))^{2}.

Proof.

For the convexity, if ρti∈Π⁡(μti,νti)\rho^{i}_{t}\in\Pi(\mu^{i}_{t},\nu^{i}_{t}) for every t∈[0,1],i∈{0,1}t\in[0,1],i\in\{0,1\}, then (1−s)​ρt0+s​ρt1∈Π⁡(μts,νts)(1-s)\rho^{0}_{t}+s\rho^{1}_{t}\in\Pi(\mu^{s}_{t},\nu^{s}_{t}) for every t,s∈[0,1]t,s\in[0,1], where μts:=(1−s)​μt0+s​μt1\mu^{s}_{t}:=(1-s)\mu_{t}^{0}+s\mu_{t}^{1} and νts:=(1−s)​νt0+s​νt1\nu^{s}_{t}:=(1-s)\nu^{0}_{t}+s\nu^{1}_{t}. Leveraging the convexity of the relative Fisher information, we can then consider convex combinations of minimizers and reproduce [11, Proof of Lemma 12] without any change.

For the lower-semicontinuity, if ρ(n)∈Π⁡(μ(n),ν(n))\rho^{(n)}\in\Pi(\mu^{(n)},\nu^{(n)}), ρ(n)→ρ\rho^{(n)}\to\rho, μ(n)→μ\mu^{(n)}\to\mu and ν(n)→ν\nu^{(n)}\to\nu for the weak convergence of measures, then it is direct that ρ∈Π⁡(μ,ν)\rho\in\Pi(\mu,\nu). Since 𝒜ε\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon} is lower-semicontinuous with respect to the pointwise-in-time convergence, we can then substitute 𝓗ν\boldsymbol{\mathcal{H}}_{\nu} with 𝒜ε\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon} in [11, Proof of Lemma 12], and the result follows from the exact same arguments. ∎

Appendix A Appendix: entropy minimization on path space

This appendix informally sketches the connection between the regularized problem (15) and its entropic minimization on path space formulation, which can be the thought of as the Schrödinger bridge problem restricted to the space of couplings Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu).

Let ρ0,ρ1∈Π⁡(μ,ν)\rho_{0},\ \rho_{1}\in\Pi(\mu,\nu) be fixed endpoints. Let Ω:=C⁡([0,1],ℝd×ℝd)\Omega:=C([0,1],\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}) denote the canonical space – or path space –, and let (Xt)t∈[0,1](X_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} denote the canonical process on Ω\Omega, so that the marginal law PtP_{t} at time tt of any P∈𝒫⁡(Ω)P\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega) is given by Pt=(Xt)#​PP_{t}=(X_{t})_{\#}P. We define the measure RεR^{\varepsilon} on Ω\Omega as the path law of the diffusion process in ℝd×ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d},

dZtε=ε2∇logμ⊗ν(Ztε)dt+εdBt,Z0ε∼μ⊗ν,\mathrm{d}Z_{t}^{\varepsilon}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla\log\mu\otimes\nu(Z_{t}^{\varepsilon})\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\mathrm{d}B_{t},\quad Z_{0}^{\varepsilon}\sim\mu\otimes\nu,

for a Brownian motion (Bt)t≥0(B_{t})_{t\geq 0}. Then, the entropic formulation of (15) is the minimization problem

inf{εH(P|Rε),P∈𝒫(Ω),(P0,P1)=(ρ0,ρ1),Pt∈Π(μ,ν)∀t∈(0,1)},\inf\{\varepsilon H(P|R^{\varepsilon}),\ P\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega),\ (P_{0},P_{1})=(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}),\ P_{t}\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\ \forall t\in(0,1)\}, (52)

where we recall that the pathwise entropy is defined as

H⁡(P|Rε):={∫Ωlogd​Pd​RεdP,if​P≪Rε,+∞otherwise.H(P|R^{\varepsilon}):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\log\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}R^{\varepsilon}}\mathrm{d}P,\quad&\text{if}\ P\ll R^{\varepsilon},\\ +\infty\quad&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The precise connection between both formulations is informally stated below.

Proposition A.1 (Informal).

Let ρ0,ρ1∈Π⁡(μ,ν)\rho_{0},\rho_{1}\in\Pi(\mu,\nu) be such that H⁡(ρ0|μ⊗ν),H⁡(ρ1|μ⊗ν)<+∞H(\rho_{0}|\mu\otimes\nu),\ H(\rho_{1}|\mu\otimes\nu)<+\infty. Then (15) and (52) are equivalent after minimizing over path measures. More precisely, for any Markovian path measure P∈𝒫⁡(Ω)P\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega) such that (P0,P1)=(ρ0,ρ1)(P_{0},P_{1})=(\rho_{0},\rho_{1}) and Pt∈Π⁡(μ,ν)​∀t∈[0,1]P_{t}\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\ \forall t\in[0,1], we have

ε​H​(P|Rε)≥𝒜ε​(P⋅)+ε​H⁡(ρ0|μ⊗ν)+H⁡(ρ1|μ⊗ν)2.\varepsilon H(P|R^{\varepsilon})\geq\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon}(P_{\cdot})+\varepsilon\frac{H(\rho_{0}|\mu\otimes\nu)+H(\rho_{1}|\mu\otimes\nu)}{2}.

where (P⋅)=(Pt)0≤t≤1(P_{\cdot})=(P_{t})_{0\leq t\leq 1} is the curve of the time-marginals of PP, and 𝒜ε\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon} is introduced in Definition 2.4. Under the usual finite-entropy hypotheses, equality is recovered after minimizing over path measures with prescribed marginal curve.

This statement can be made rigorous using the (probabilistic) Girsanov theory under finite entropy condition [43] – although this goes beyond the scope of the present work. We refer to [44] for a rigorous discussion of such pathwise formulations in the context of the Schrödinger bridge problem, and to [48] and [11, Section 3] in the context of the Brödinger problem. We finally emphasize the convenience of the entropic formulation (52), which directly benefits from the nice properties of the relative entropy – such as lower semicontinuity, strict convexity and compactness of level sets –, although (15) was more adequate to derive a complete PDE description of optimality conditions.
